title: Freelance Project Status Update Kit
description: Keep every client informed in 15 minutes a week. Three fill-in update formats, six weeks of real-looking updates for one project (including a slip and recovery), clear Green/Amber/Red rules, nine same-day emails for delays, mistakes, budget warnings and late client inputs, a Friday routine and a weekly status tracker with example rows.

files.README.md:
# Freelance Project Status Update Kit

Clients rarely fire freelancers for being late. They fire them for being
quiet. This kit gives you a 15-minute weekly habit that keeps every client
informed, surfaces problems while they are still small, and leaves a
written record you can point back to if a project goes sideways.

## What's inside

| File | What it's for | Time needed |
|---|---|---|
| status-update-templates.md | Three fill-in update formats: quick, standard weekly and milestone | Copy as needed |
| worked-example.md | Six real-looking weekly updates for one project, including a slip and a recovery | 10 min read |
| traffic-light-guide.md | Clear rules for calling a project Green, Amber or Red, so you never under-report | 10 min read |
| bad-news-emails.md | Nine emails for delays, budget warnings, mistakes, illness and slipping client inputs | Copy as needed |
| friday-update-routine.md | The 15-minute end-of-week routine that produces every update | 15 min a week |
| status-tracker.csv | One row per project per week: status, progress, waiting-on, risks, next date | 2 min per project |

## How to use it

1. **Today (20 minutes):** read `traffic-light-guide.md` and
   `worked-example.md`. Pick one format from `status-update-templates.md`
   for each active client. Small or low-touch clients get the quick format,
   most get the standard weekly, and big multi-phase projects get the
   milestone format at each phase.
2. **Tell each client when to expect updates.** One line is enough:
   "You'll get a short written update from me every Friday afternoon, so
   you always know where things stand without needing to ask."
3. **Open `status-tracker.csv`** in Excel, Google Sheets or Numbers. Delete
   the example rows (they start with "Example") once you've seen how they
   work.
4. **Every Friday,** follow `friday-update-routine.md`. Fill the tracker
   first, then write the updates from it. It takes about 3 minutes per
   project once you're used to it.
5. **When something goes wrong,** don't wait for Friday. Use
   `bad-news-emails.md` the same day you know.

## The five rules behind the kit

1. **Same day, same format, every week.** Predictability is what makes
   clients relax. An update that arrives every Friday is worth more than a
   brilliant one that arrives when you remember.
2. **Lead with the status, not the story.** The first line says whether
   the project is on track. Details come after.
3. **Always name what you're waiting on.** Most delays on freelance
   projects are caused by missing client input. Writing it down every week
   is fair, polite and protects your deadline.
4. **Bad news travels early.** A delay you flag two weeks out is a
   planning change. The same delay flagged the day before is a broken
   promise.
5. **Every update ends with a date.** The next deliverable, the next
   decision or the next update. Never end on "let me know if you have any
   questions" alone.

## Works with

Any email client, Excel, Google Sheets, Numbers or LibreOffice. No
software to buy and no account to create.

# Status Update Templates

Three formats. Replace everything in [brackets]. Delete any section that
has nothing in it this week, except "Waiting on you" and "Next": write
"Nothing" there rather than removing them, so the client learns to look
for them.

---

## Format 1: Quick update (small projects, under 3 weeks)

Use when the client wants to know "is it fine?" and nothing more.

**Subject:** [Project] - week of [date]: [On track / Slight delay / Needs a decision]

Hi [Name],

Quick update on [project]: **[on track for (date) / running about (X)
days behind, new date (date) / blocked until (thing) arrives]**.

This week I [one sentence on what got done].
Next week I'll [one sentence on what's next].
From you I need: [specific thing, by (day)] / Nothing this week.

[Your name]

---

## Format 2: Standard weekly update (most projects)

**Subject:** [Project] update - [date] - [Green / Amber / Red]

Hi [Name],

**Status: [Green - on track / Amber - at risk / Red - off track]**
[One sentence that explains the colour. Example: "On track for the
(date) launch." or "At risk: we need the product photos by Tuesday to
keep the (date) date."]

**Done this week**
- [Finished item, written as an outcome the client cares about]
- [Finished item]

**Next week**
- [Planned item] - [day you expect it done]
- [Planned item]

**Waiting on you**
- [Specific item] - needed by [day/date] - [what it affects if late]
- Nothing this week

**Decisions needed**
- [Question with options. Example: "Do you want the pricing table on the
  homepage (option A) or only on the Pricing page (option B)? I
  recommend B because (reason)."]

**Budget / hours** *(only if the client pays by the hour or has a cap)*
- Used [X] of [Y] hours ([Z]%). Expected total: [N] hours.

**Next update:** [day, date]. Next thing you'll see: [deliverable] on
[date].

[Your name]

---

## Format 3: Milestone update (end of a phase, or monthly on big projects)

**Subject:** [Project] - [phase name] complete / milestone report

Hi [Name],

**Where we are**
[Phase] is [complete / complete except (item)]. Overall the project is
[Green/Amber/Red]: [one-sentence reason].

**What this phase delivered**
| Deliverable | Status | Where to find it |
|---|---|---|
| [Item] | Approved / Awaiting your approval / Delivered | [Folder or attachment name] |
| [Item] | | |

**Timeline**
| Milestone | Original date | Current date | Note |
|---|---|---|---|
| [Phase 1] | [date] | [date] | Done |
| [Phase 2] | [date] | [date] | [On track / moved because ...] |
| [Launch / final delivery] | [date] | [date] | |

**Budget**
[Fixed price: "No change to the agreed fee of (amount)." or "One approved
change (CR-01) adds (amount); new total (amount)."]
[Hourly: "(X) of (Y) hours used. Forecast to finish at (N) hours."]

**Risks I'm watching**
1. [Risk] - likelihood [low/medium/high] - what I'm doing about it.
2. [Risk]

**What I need from you before the next phase starts**
- [Approval / content / access] by [date]

**Invoice**
[If a milestone payment is due: "As agreed, the (phase) invoice for
(amount) is attached, due (date)."]

**Next phase starts:** [date]. First thing you'll see: [deliverable] on
[date].

[Your name]

---

## Phrases that help

**Saying something is done without overclaiming**
- "Ready for your review" (not "finished") until the client approves.
- "Drafted" / "Built" / "Approved" / "Live": use the same four words every
  week so status is unambiguous.

**Naming client delays without blame**
- "To keep the [date] date, I'll need [item] by [day]."
- "[Item] hasn't arrived yet, so I've moved on to [other task] in the
  meantime. If it arrives by [day], we're still on track."
- "Because [item] arrived on [date] instead of [date], [deliverable] will
  now land on [new date]."

**Asking for a decision**
- Give two or three options, your recommendation and a reason, and a
  default: "If I don't hear back by Wednesday, I'll go with B so we keep
  moving."
  Only use a default where either option is easy to reverse.

**Avoid**
- "Just checking in" with nothing new to say.
- Percent-complete numbers without a definition ("80% done" means nothing
  to a client and usually means 50%).
- Burying a delay in the third paragraph.

# Worked Example: Six Weeks of Updates

The project: a freelance web designer, Alex, is rebuilding the five-page
website for a small (fictional) physiotherapy clinic. Fixed fee $4,800,
paid 40% / 30% / 30%. Six-week plan, launch on Friday 18 December. The
client contact is the practice manager, Jo.

The plan agreed at kickoff:

| Week | Work | Needs from client |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Sitemap, wireframes | Logo files, current site login |
| 2 | Homepage design | Feedback on wireframes |
| 3 | Inner page designs | Approval of homepage, team photos |
| 4 | Build | Final page text |
| 5 | Build, content entry | |
| 6 | Testing, launch | Final sign-off |

Watch how the "Waiting on you" section does most of the work, and how the
week 4 slip is reported before it becomes a missed launch.

---

## Week 1 - Friday 13 November

**Subject:** Clinic website update - 13 Nov - Green

Hi Jo,

**Status: Green - on track for the 18 December launch.**

**Done this week**
- Sitemap agreed on our Tuesday call (five pages plus a booking page).
- Wireframes for all six pages: attached as a PDF.

**Next week**
- Homepage design, first version - Thursday.

**Waiting on you**
- Feedback on the wireframes - by Tuesday 17 Nov, so I can start the
  homepage design on the right layout.
- Logo files (ideally the original files from your designer, or the
  largest version you have) - by Tuesday.

**Decisions needed**
- Nothing this week.

**Next update:** Friday 20 November.

Alex

---

## Week 2 - Friday 20 November

**Subject:** Clinic website update - 20 Nov - Green

Hi Jo,

**Status: Green - on track for 18 December.**

**Done this week**
- Wireframes approved (thanks for the quick notes).
- Homepage design, version 1: attached. I've used the logo files you sent
  and the colours from your printed leaflets.

**Next week**
- Homepage changes from your feedback - Tuesday.
- Inner page designs (Services, About, Team, Contact) - Friday.

**Waiting on you**
- Homepage feedback - by Tuesday 24 Nov. Please send it as one list from
  you and Dr Patel together, so I don't get conflicting notes.
- Team photos - by Friday 27 Nov. If a new photo shoot isn't possible,
  current photos are fine as long as they're at least 1200 pixels wide.

**Decisions needed**
- Should "Book an appointment" go to your existing booking system or to
  a contact form? I recommend your booking system: fewer steps for
  patients and no double entry for reception.

**Next update:** Friday 27 November.

Alex

---

## Week 3 - Friday 27 November

**Subject:** Clinic website update - 27 Nov - Amber

Hi Jo,

**Status: Amber - launch date at risk.** Everything on my side is on
schedule, but I need the page text by Wednesday 2 December to build in
week 5 and still launch on 18 December.

**Done this week**
- Homepage approved.
- Inner page designs: attached for review.
- Booking button connected to your booking system (test link included).

**Next week**
- Start building the site from the approved designs - Monday.
- Inner page changes from your feedback - Wednesday.

**Waiting on you**
- Final page text for all five pages - **by Wednesday 2 Dec.** This is
  now the one thing that decides the launch date.
- Inner page feedback - by Tuesday 1 Dec.
- Team photos - not received yet. If they're not ready, I'll build with
  placeholder silhouettes and swap them in after launch at no charge.

**Decisions needed**
- Nothing new.

**Invoice:** As agreed, the second payment ($1,440) is attached, due
11 December.

**Next update:** Friday 4 December.

Alex

*Why Amber and not Green?* Alex's work is on schedule, but the project
isn't. The traffic light reports the project, not the freelancer.

---

## Week 4 - Wednesday 2 December (not a Friday update)

The text didn't arrive. Alex sends a short email the same day rather than
waiting for Friday. (This is email 5 from `bad-news-emails.md`.)

**Subject:** Clinic website - page text and the launch date

Hi Jo,

I haven't received the page text yet, so I want to give you the options
now while there's still room to choose.

1. **Text by Monday 7 Dec:** I can still launch on 18 December, but
   there'd be no buffer for late changes.
2. **Text by Friday 11 Dec:** launch moves to Wednesday 23 December.
3. **Launch on 18 December with the current site's text,** lightly edited
   by me, and swap in the new text in January. This keeps the date but
   the text won't be final.

If none of these work, let's have a quick call. Could you let me know
which you prefer by Friday?

Alex

---

## Week 4 - Friday 4 December

**Subject:** Clinic website update - 4 Dec - Amber

Hi Jo,

**Status: Amber.** Thanks for choosing option 1. Launch stays on
18 December, provided the text arrives by Monday 7 December.

**Done this week**
- Inner page designs approved.
- Site build started: homepage and Services page are built on the test
  site (link and login in our shared folder).

**Next week**
- Add your text and images to all pages - Wednesday.
- Full test site ready for your review - Friday 11 December.

**Waiting on you**
- Final page text - **by Monday 7 Dec** (option 1).
- Team photos - by Monday 7 Dec, otherwise placeholders as discussed.

**Next update:** Friday 11 December.

Alex

---

## Week 5 - Friday 11 December

**Subject:** Clinic website update - 11 Dec - Green

Hi Jo,

**Status: Green - back on track for 18 December.** The text arrived on
Monday, so we're good.

**Done this week**
- All five pages built with your text and photos.
- Test site ready for your review (link in the shared folder).
- Tested on phone, tablet and desktop, and in the three main browsers.

**Next week**
- Changes from your review - Tuesday.
- Launch - Friday 18 December, 10am (quiet time for your bookings).

**Waiting on you**
- Review of the test site - **by Monday 14 Dec.** One combined list,
  please.
- Written sign-off to launch - by Thursday 17 Dec (a reply saying
  "approved for launch" is enough).

**Decisions needed**
- Do you want the old site's address for the blog to redirect to the new
  News page? I recommend yes, so old links keep working.

**Next update:** launch day.

Alex

---

## Week 6 - Friday 18 December

**Subject:** Clinic website is live

Hi Jo,

**The new site is live.** Everything from your review list is done, and
the booking button is working (I made one test booking and cancelled it).

**What you have**
- The live site, and a 10-minute walkthrough video on updating text and
  photos (in the shared folder).
- Your login details, sent separately.

**What happens next**
- I'll check the site daily for the next week.
- The final invoice ($1,440) is attached, due 1 January.
- 30 days of fixes for anything that isn't working as designed are
  included, until 17 January.

Thank you for all the quick feedback. It was a pleasure.

Alex

---

## What made these updates work

- **Every update had the status in the subject line.** Jo could tell from
  her inbox whether she needed to act.
- **"Waiting on you" appeared every week**, with a date and a consequence.
  When the text was late, nobody was surprised.
- **The slip was reported on the day it happened, with options.** The
  client chose the trade-off; Alex didn't have to absorb it.
- **Amber was used honestly.** It turned Green again only when the cause
  was fixed.
- **Invoices were mentioned in the update**, so payment felt like part of
  the plan rather than a separate demand.

# Traffic Light Guide: Green, Amber, Red

Most freelancers report Green until the day they report Red. These rules
stop that. Decide the colour by answering the questions below, not by how
you feel about the project.

## The definitions

**Green: on track.**
The next milestone and the final date will be met with the time and money
agreed, and nothing you're waiting on is overdue.

**Amber: at risk.**
At least one thing could move a date or the budget if it isn't sorted
within a week, but there is still a clear way to recover without changing
the plan. Amber always comes with "what would make it Green again".

**Red: off track.**
A date or the budget will change unless the client makes a decision or
something outside your control changes. Red always comes with options.

## The six-question test

Answer each question every Friday. The worst answer sets the colour.

| # | Question | Green | Amber | Red |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Will the next milestone be delivered on its agreed date? | Yes | Only if something specific happens this week | No |
| 2 | Is anything you need from the client overdue? | No | Overdue by up to 3 working days | Overdue by more than 3 working days, or it now affects a date |
| 3 | Hours or costs used vs. progress (hourly or capped projects) | Within 10% of plan | 10-25% over plan | More than 25% over, or the cap will be passed |
| 4 | Is there an open question about scope that you haven't agreed yet? | No | Yes, raised with the client | Yes, and it changes cost or date |
| 5 | Has the final date had to move already? | No | Moved once, with the client's agreement, and holding | Likely to move again |
| 6 | Are you confident in your own capacity for the next two weeks? | Yes | Tight, but planned | No (illness, overbooking, other client emergency) |

## Rules of thumb

- **Report the project, not yourself.** If your work is on time but the
  client's input is late, the project is Amber. That's not blame; it's
  information they need.
- **Never go from Green straight to Red** unless something sudden
  happened (illness, a tool failure, a client decision). If you find
  yourself doing it often, you're reporting too optimistically.
- **Amber for more than three weeks in a row is Red.** Something isn't
  being fixed.
- **Only turn back to Green when the cause is gone**, not when you feel
  better about it.
- **Red needs a same-day email**, not a line in Friday's update. Use the
  templates in `bad-news-emails.md`.

## What to write with each colour

**Green:** one line. "On track for [date]."

**Amber:** the risk, the date it becomes a problem, and what turns it
Green. "At risk: if the product photos arrive by Tuesday, we stay on
track for [date]."

**Red:** what has changed, why, the new reality, and two or three options
with your recommendation. Ask for a decision by a specific date.

## Example colours from real-world situations

| Situation | Colour | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Everything delivered on time, client feedback came back a day early | Green | Nothing at risk |
| Client feedback is two days late, final date still has a week of buffer | Amber | Overdue input, recoverable |
| You underestimated a feature by 6 hours on a 60-hour fixed-fee project | Green or Amber | Green if you'll absorb it and dates hold; Amber if dates are tight |
| Client asked for a new page; you've sent a quote but not had a reply | Amber | Open scope question raised |
| You've been ill for four days and the review date is Monday | Red | A date will move |
| Hourly project at 70% of the hour cap with half the work done | Red | The cap will be passed without a decision |
| Client contact went on holiday without approving the design | Amber, then Red after 3 working days | Approval overdue |
files.bad-news-emails.md:
# Bad News Emails

Nine emails for the moments most freelancers put off. Send them the same
day you know, not at the next scheduled update. Replace everything in
[brackets].

**The structure every one of these follows**

1. Say the news in the first two lines.
2. Say why, briefly, without excuses or over-apologising.
3. Give the new reality: a date, a number, or options.
4. Say what you're doing about it.
5. Ask for one specific thing, by a specific date.

---

## 1. Your own delay (you underestimated the work)

**Subject:** [Project] - [deliverable] moving to [new date]

Hi [Name],

I need to move the [deliverable] from [original date] to [new date].

[One sentence of honest reason. Example: "The booking integration has
taken longer than I estimated because your system needs a separate
setup for each practitioner."]

The rest of the timeline is [unchanged / moving by the same (X) days:
new final date (date)]. There's no change to the fee.

To make up some of the time, I'll [specific action: send the pages that
are ready on (date) so you can start reviewing early].

Sorry for the change. If [new date] causes a problem on your side, tell
me and we'll work out what to prioritise.

[Your name]

---

## 2. Delay caused by illness or emergency

**Subject:** [Project] - short delay this week

Hi [Name],

I've been [unwell / dealing with a family emergency] since [day] and
haven't been able to work on [project]. I'm [back from (day) / expecting
to be back by (day)].

The new date for [deliverable] is [date]. [Optional: The final date of
(date) still holds / moves to (date).]

I'll send a full update on [day]. If anything urgent comes up before
then, [how to reach you or who to contact].

[Your name]

*Tip: you don't owe the client medical details. "Unwell" is enough.*

---

## 3. Early budget warning (hourly or capped projects)

**Subject:** [Project] - hours check before we go further

Hi [Name],

A heads-up on hours before it becomes a problem: we've used [X] of the
[Y] hours budgeted, and I estimate the remaining work will take [Z]
hours, which would bring the total to [X+Z], about [N] over the budget.

The main reason is [scope change / more revision rounds than planned /
technical issue].

Options:
1. **Increase the budget to [amount]** and finish everything as planned.
2. **Keep the budget** and drop or simplify [specific items].
3. **Pause after [milestone]** and decide on the rest later.

I recommend [option] because [reason]. I'll keep working on [items not
affected] until I hear from you, and won't go past [Y] hours without your
OK. Could you let me know by [date]?

[Your name]

---

## 4. You made a mistake

**Subject:** [Project] - error in [deliverable], now fixed

Hi [Name],

I found an error in [deliverable] I sent on [date]: [what was wrong, in
one plain sentence].

[It's now fixed: corrected version attached / live.] [Or: I'm fixing it
now and will have it corrected by (time).]

[If it affected anything already used:] It may have affected [what], so
I'd suggest [specific action]. I'm happy to [help with that / do that for
you] at no charge.

To stop this happening again, I've [added a check / changed my process].

Sorry for the trouble.

[Your name]

*Tip: tell the client before they find it. A mistake you report is a
sign of care; a mistake they find is a sign of carelessness.*

---

## 5. Client input is late and now affects the date

**Subject:** [Project] - [missing item] and the [launch/delivery] date

Hi [Name],

I haven't received [item] yet, and it's now the thing that decides the
[launch/delivery] date, so I want to give you the options while there's
still room to choose:

1. **[Item] by [date]:** we keep [original date].
2. **[Item] by [later date]:** [delivery] moves to [new date].
3. **[A workaround, e.g. launch with placeholder text and update
   later]:** we keep the date, but [trade-off].

Could you let me know which works best by [date]? If it's easier, I can
[draft the item for you to edit / jump on a 10-minute call].

[Your name]

---

## 6. Waiting on approval before the next phase

**Subject:** [Project] - approval needed to start [next phase]

Hi [Name],

[Phase] is ready and waiting for your approval before I start [next
phase]. To keep [date], I'll need a yes (or your changes) by [day].

A reply saying "approved" is all I need. If you'd like changes, one
combined list is the fastest way.

[Your name]

---

## 7. A third party has caused a problem

**Subject:** [Project] - issue with [supplier/tool/platform]

Hi [Name],

[Supplier/tool] [what happened, e.g. "has changed how their booking
widget works, so the connection I built stopped working on Wednesday"].
Your [site/project] is [still working / partly affected: (what)].

What I'm doing: [steps]. I expect it to be fixed by [date].

[If it costs time or money:] Fixing this will take about [X] hours. As
it's outside the original scope, [I'll cover it / it would be (amount);
let me know if you'd like me to go ahead].

[Your name]

---

## 8. The project needs to be re-planned

**Subject:** [Project] - proposing a revised plan

Hi [Name],

The project has changed enough since we started that the original plan no
longer fits: [two or three bullet points of what changed].

Rather than keep patching dates, I'd like to agree a revised plan.
Attached is a one-page version with:
- the work still to do,
- new dates for each milestone,
- [any change to the fee, with the reason].

Could we talk it through on [day/time options]? It'll take 20 minutes.

[Your name]

---

## 9. Good news that comes with a catch

**Subject:** [Project] - [deliverable] ready early, one thing to check

Hi [Name],

Good news: [deliverable] is ready [X days] early.

One thing to check before you approve: [issue or assumption, e.g. "I've
used the prices from your current site. If they're changing in January,
let me know and I'll update them before launch"].

[Your name]
files.friday-update-routine.md:
# The Friday Update Routine (15 minutes)

Block 15 minutes every Friday afternoon in your calendar as a recurring
appointment. Add 3 minutes for every active project beyond three.

## Before you start: one-time setup (10 minutes)

- [ ] Make one email draft per client from
      `status-update-templates.md` and save it as a template or a note
      you can copy.
- [ ] Open `status-tracker.csv` and add one row per active project.
- [ ] Tell every client which day updates arrive.

## The routine

### 1. Fill the tracker first (1 minute per project)

For each project, add a new row in `status-tracker.csv`:

- [ ] What got finished this week (outcomes, not activities).
- [ ] What's planned next week, with days.
- [ ] Anything you're waiting on, the date it was due and what it
      affects.
- [ ] Hours used vs. budget, if relevant.
- [ ] The colour, using the six-question test in
      `traffic-light-guide.md`.

Writing the tracker first means you decide the colour before you start
choosing friendly words.

### 2. Check last week's promises (2 minutes)

- [ ] Look at last week's "Next week" column for each project. Did each
      item happen? If not, it goes in this week's update with a new day.
- [ ] Look at last week's "Waiting on" column. Anything still missing?
      It becomes more specific this week: add the consequence.

### 3. Write the updates (1-2 minutes per project)

- [ ] Copy the template. Fill it from the tracker row.
- [ ] Status and colour in the subject line.
- [ ] One clear sentence explaining the colour.
- [ ] "Waiting on you" with dates, or "Nothing this week".
- [ ] End with the date of the next update and the next deliverable.

### 4. The 20-second read-through

Read each update as if you were the client reading it on a phone between
meetings:

- [ ] Can they tell in the first line whether they need to act?
- [ ] Is every request specific (what, by when)?
- [ ] Is there any jargon you can swap for plain words?
- [ ] Is there anything you'd be embarrassed to have forwarded to their
      boss? Fix it.

### 5. Send, then file (1 minute)

- [ ] Send all updates before the end of your working day.
- [ ] Save a copy in each project's folder (or keep them in one email
      thread per project). These become your record if there's ever a
      dispute about dates or delays.
- [ ] Put any follow-ups in your calendar: for each "Waiting on you" item,
      a reminder on the day it's due.

## When there's nothing to report

Still send it. Two lines is enough:

> Quiet week on [project]: still on track for [date]. Next update [date].
> Nothing needed from you.

A short update keeps the habit alive and still shows the client you're
paying attention.

## When a client says "you don't need to send these"

Some clients genuinely prefer less email. Offer the quick format, or a
fortnightly update instead. Keep filling in the tracker for yourself, and
keep sending same-day emails for Amber-to-Red changes and anything that
affects dates or money.

## Monthly add-on (10 minutes, last Friday of the month)

- [ ] Filter the tracker by project. How many weeks was each one Amber or
      Red? What caused it?
- [ ] Which client inputs were late most often? Build more buffer for
      that client next time, or ask for those inputs earlier.
